subject: Biology
title: Reproduction (KPK Board)
learningOutcomes: Define reproduction and describe its importance.
Describe different types of asexual reproduction, i.e. binary fission, budding, spore formation and vegetative propagation.
Distinguish between vegetative propagation and artificial propagation.
Explain vegetative propagation in plants (through stem, suckers and leaves).
Describe the two methods of artificial vegetative propagation (stem cuttings and grafting).
Define cloning.
Describe sexual reproduction in plants by explaining the life cycle of a flowering plant.
Describe the adaptations in the structure of wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers.
Describe the structure of a seed.
Distinguish between epigeal and hypogeal germination.
Describe the conditions necessary for germination of seeds.
State the contributions of Theophrastus in the discovery of sex in plants.
Rationalise how parthenogenesis is a type of asexual reproduction.
Outline binary fission, multiple fission, budding and fragmentation as asexual methods of reproduction in animals.
Define fertilisation and differentiate between external and internal fertilisation.
Describe different organs of the male and female reproductive systems of a rabbit.
Describe the process of gametogenesis in a rabbit.
Rationalise the need for population planning.
Explain AIDS as an example of sexually transmitted diseases.
State the role of the National AIDS Control Programme and different NGOs in educating people with reference to AIDS.

sections.heading: Reproduction and its Types
sections.body: Reproduction is the process by which living organisms produce new organisms of their own kind. It ensures the continuity of a species by transmitting genetic material from one generation to the next. An individual can live without reproduction, but a species cannot survive without it. There are two main types of reproduction: asexual and sexual. Asexual reproduction involves no fusion of gametes and usually only a single parent; the offspring are similar to the parent and show no genetic variation, so they are called clones. Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes of two parents; the offspring receive a blend of characteristics from both parents and therefore show variation. Asexual reproduction does not create genetic variation.

sections.heading: Asexual Reproduction in Unicellular Organisms
sections.body: In binary fission the body of the parent divides into two daughter organisms. In bacteria the DNA molecule first duplicates to form two DNA molecules that move to opposite sides, then the cell wall and membrane constrict from both sides and meet in the centre, separating the cell into two daughter cells. In protists such as Euglena, Amoeba and Chlamydomonas the nucleus divides into two, followed by division of the cytoplasm, giving two daughter cells of almost equal size. In multiple fission, which occurs during unfavourable conditions, the nucleus divides repeatedly to form many daughter cells from one parent cell, inside a protective covering called a cyst (Amoeba and Plasmodium). In budding, an outgrowth called a bud arises from the parent and grows into an offspring, as in yeast and Hydra. Fungi such as Rhizopus (bread mould) reproduce by spore formation: thick-walled spores are produced in sporangia and resist adverse conditions. Bacteria form endospores inside their cells when conditions are harsh.

sections.heading: Vegetative Propagation, Artificial Propagation and Cloning
sections.body: In vegetative propagation a plant produces new plants from its vegetative parts: stems, leaves and roots. Natural examples are the stolon or runner of strawberry, the rhizome of ginger and ferns, the bulb of onion, tulip and lily, the corm of Colocasia and garlic, the tuber of potato whose axillary buds are called eyes, the suckers (root sprouts) of red raspberry and the leaf buds of Bryophyllum. Artificial vegetative propagation uses methods developed by humans, mainly cutting and grafting. In cutting, pieces of stem (grape vine, rose, chrysanthemum) or root (sweet potato, blackberries) are cut and used to grow new plants. In grafting, a branch of a desired variety is attached to the stem of an ordinary plant to get fruit of better quality and quantity; almond, plum and cherries are propagated this way. Cloning is an asexual technique in which a population of genetically identical individuals is produced from the tissues or cells of a single parent, which helps preserve the quality of the yield and increase agricultural output.

sections.heading: The Flower and the Life Cycle of a Flowering Plant
sections.body: A flower is borne on the receptacle, the swollen tip of the flower stalk. It has four whorls: the calyx (sepals, outermost, usually green and protective), the corolla (petals, usually coloured), the androecium (stamens, each with an anther and a filament) and the gynoecium (carpels, each with an ovary, style and stigma). The anther contains pollen sacs (microsporangia) producing microspores; the ovules (megasporangia) in the ovary produce megaspores. Bisexual flowers have stamens and carpels together; unisexual flowers have them in separate flowers. A flowering plant shows alternation of generations: the diploid sporophyte (2n) alternates with the haploid gametophyte (n). A diploid megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis into four haploid megaspores; one survives and divides by mitosis into eight nuclei that form the seven-celled embryo sac (egg, fusion nucleus and five non-functional cells). A microspore develops into the pollen grain, a two-celled male gametophyte with a tube cell and a generative cell.

sections.heading: Pollination, Fertilisation, Seed and Germination
sections.body: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. Self-pollination involves one flower or flowers of the same plant; cross-pollination involves two flowers of different plants of the same species. Insect-pollinated flowers have brightly coloured large petals, fragrance, nectar, sticky pollen and sticky or specially shaped stigmas; wind-pollinated flowers have no scent or nectar, small smooth winged pollen, feathery stigmas, large anthers on long stalks and pollen produced in large numbers. The tube cell forms the pollen tube, which enters the ovule through the micropyle, and the generative cell forms two sperms. In double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants, one sperm fuses with the egg to form the zygote and the other with the fusion nucleus to form the triploid (3n) endosperm. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit. A seed has a seed coat (testa), hilum, micropyle, an embryo (plumule, radicle, epicotyl, hypocotyl, cotyledons) and, in monocots, endosperm. Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature (5 to 30 °C); it is epigeal when the hypocotyl lifts the cotyledons above ground (melon, cucumber, bean) and hypogeal when the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons stay below ground (maize, pea). Theophrastus, the father of botany, discovered sex in plants.

sections.heading: Reproduction in Animals
sections.body: Animals reproduce asexually by fragmentation (Planaria), budding (Hydra) and parthenogenesis, in which an unfertilised egg develops into a new organism; in honeybees fertilised eggs become females and unfertilised eggs become males. Most animals reproduce sexually. Gonads (testes and ovaries) produce gametes and sex hormones. Gametogenesis is the formation of gametes by meiosis, which reduces the chromosome number from diploid to haploid. In spermatogenesis each diploid primary spermatocyte in the testes forms four haploid spermatids, which develop into motile sperms. In oogenesis a diploid primary oocyte in a follicle of the ovary forms a secondary oocyte and a first polar body in meiosis I, then an egg and a second polar body in meiosis II. Fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote, which restores the diploid number. It is external in fish and amphibians (many gametes are released because chances of loss in water are high) and internal in reptiles, birds and mammals. In the male rabbit the testes lie in the scrotum and sperms form in the seminiferous tubules; the epididymis, sperm ducts and urethra carry them, helped by the seminal vesicle, prostate and Cowper’s glands. The female has ovaries, oviducts, a two-horned uterus, cervices and the birth canal (vagina).

sections.heading: Population Planning, STDs and AIDS
sections.body: According to the 2017 census Pakistan has nearly 208 million people. Rapid population growth puts great pressure on agricultural land and resources and hinders economic and social development, so population planning is needed. It includes an effective family planning programme, changing social attitudes and improving the status of women; lowering the growth rate became a permanent feature of Pakistan’s five-year plans by the early 1990s. Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs, also called STIs) are infections acquired through sexual activity with infected people. AIDS is a viral infection caused by the Human Immuno-deficiency Virus (HIV), which attacks the white blood cells that kill pathogens and so weakens the body’s defence system. HIV spreads through body fluids during sexual activity, infected needles and transfusion of infected blood. There is no cure, but antiretroviral drugs hinder the growth of HIV. The National AIDS Control Programme runs a comprehensive programme to halt the epidemic and educates people, parliamentarians, media and religious leaders, with events such as World AIDS Day; NGOs coordinate prevention and control activities.

definitions.definition: The process by which living organisms produce new organisms of their own kind.
Reproduction without the fusion of gametes, usually involving a single parent.
Reproduction in which the male and female gametes of two parents fuse to produce offspring.
An offspring of asexual reproduction that is genetically identical to its single parent.
Asexual reproduction in which the body of the parent divides into two daughter organisms.
Asexual reproduction in which the nucleus divides repeatedly to form many daughter cells from one parent cell.
A protective covering formed over the cell during multiple fission.
Asexual reproduction in which an outgrowth called a bud arises from the parent and grows into an offspring.
Asexual reproduction in which organisms such as fungi make thick-walled spores in sporangia.
A thick-walled sac in which spores are produced.
Spores formed inside bacterial cells when conditions are harsh.
Asexual reproduction in which a plant produces new plants from its stems, leaves or roots.
A horizontal stem that grows above the ground and forms new plantlets at its nodes, e.g. strawberry.
A horizontal underground stem that gives rise to new plants, e.g. ginger and ferns.
An underground bud with fleshy leaves that store food, e.g. onion, tulip and lily.
An underground stem like a bulb but without fleshy leaves, e.g. Colocasia and garlic.
An underground, swollen, fleshy stem with buds called eyes, e.g. potato.
A method in which pieces of stem or root are cut from a plant to grow new plants.
A method in which a branch of a desired variety is attached to the stem of an ordinary plant to get better quality fruit.
A technique in which genetically identical individuals are produced from the tissues or cells of a single parent.
The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower.
The fusion of two sperms, one with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus; unique to flowering plants.
A triploid (3n) tissue formed when the second sperm fuses with the fusion nucleus; it nourishes the embryo.
Development of the ovary into a fruit without fertilisation, giving a seedless fruit.
A mature ovule: a miniature plant with a protective cover in a suspended state of development.
The development of the embryo of a seed into a seedling.
Germination in which the hypocotyl elongates and brings the cotyledons above the ground.
Germination in which the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons remain below the ground.
A special type of asexual reproduction in which an unfertilised egg develops into a new organism.
A method in which the body of an organism breaks into fragments, each of which develops into a new organism.
The formation of gametes in the gonads by meiosis.
The fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote.
The first cell of a new offspring, formed by fertilisation.
A life cycle in which a diploid sporophyte generation alternates with a haploid gametophyte generation.
Sexually transmitted disease: an infection acquired through sexual activity with an infected person.
Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, a viral infection caused by HIV.

examTips: Compare asexual and sexual reproduction in a table: number of parents, fusion of gametes, variation in offspring (clones versus blend of both parents).
Learn the five asexual methods with one organism each: binary fission (Euglena, Amoeba), multiple fission (Plasmodium), budding (yeast, Hydra), spore formation (Rhizopus), fragmentation (Planaria).
For vegetative propagation remember the structure-plant pairs: stolon – strawberry, rhizome – ginger, bulb – onion, corm – Colocasia, tuber – potato, suckers – red raspberry, leaf buds – Bryophyllum.
Memorise the chromosome numbers: megaspore mother cell 2n, embryo sac and pollen grain n, zygote 2n, endosperm 3n; double fertilisation is unique to flowering plants.

Epigeal = hypocotyl elongates, cotyledons come above the ground (melon, cucumber, bean); hypogeal = epicotyl elongates, cotyledons stay below (maize, pea). Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.

Practise gametogenesis as two flow charts (spermatogenesis: 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 spermatids; oogenesis: primary oocyte → secondary oocyte + polar body → egg + second polar body) and label the rabbit reproductive systems.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which type of reproduction involves no fusion of gametes and usually only a single parent?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Asexual reproduction needs no gametes to fuse and usually involves only one parent, so the offspring are clones.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which method of asexual reproduction occurs in Plasmodium?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In multiple fission the nucleus divides repeatedly to form many daughter cells, as in Amoeba and Plasmodium.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What are the well-developed axillary buds on a potato tuber called?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A potato tuber has axillary buds called eyes above each leaf, and each eye can grow into a new potato plant.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why are fruit trees such as almond, plum and cherries propagated by grafting?

options: To make the trees grow without roots
To get fruit of better quality and quantity
To produce seedless fruit by parthenocarpy
To produce spores for the next generation

practiceQuestions.explanation: A branch of a desired variety is grafted onto an ordinary plant to obtain fruit of better quality and quantity.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which part of the stamen contains the pollen sacs (microsporangia)?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The anther contains the pollen sacs, which produce microspores; the filament only supports the anther.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In double fertilisation, what is formed when the second sperm fuses with the fusion nucleus?
practiceQuestions.explanation: One sperm fuses with the egg to form the zygote; the second fuses with the fusion nucleus to form the triploid (3n) endosperm.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In epigeal germination, which part elongates and lifts the cotyledons above the ground?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and forces the cotyledons above the ground; in hypogeal germination the epicotyl elongates.

practiceQuestions.prompt: One diploid primary spermatocyte forms four haploid spermatids. Which process makes this possible?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gametogenesis involves meiosis, which reduces the chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n).

practiceQuestions.prompt: A fish releases a very large number of eggs and sperms into the water. What is the reason?

options: Internal fertilisation guarantees survival of every gamete
The embryo develops inside the female
There are more chances of loss of gametes in water
The gametes are fertilised before they leave the body

practiceQuestions.explanation: External fertilisation takes place in water, where many gametes are lost, so animals release a large number to ensure that some fuse.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The body’s defence system of an HIV-infected person is weakened because HIV attacks which cells?
practiceQuestions.explanation: HIV attacks and destroys the white blood cells that kill pathogens, which weakens the main defence system of the body.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote is called _____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The pollen tube enters the ovule through a small opening called the _____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The pollen tube grows through the stigma and style and enters the ovule through the micropyle.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In honeybees, male bees develop from _____ eggs.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In honeybees the fertilised eggs develop into females, while the unfertilised eggs develop into males.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Double fertilisation is unique to flowering plants.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only flowering plants show double fertilisation: one sperm fuses with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Self-pollination involves two flowers of different plants of the same species.
practiceQuestions.explanation: That describes cross-pollination; self-pollination involves one flower or flowers of the same plant.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the events of seed germination in the correct order.

items: The seed absorbs water through the micropyle
The plumule grows to form the shoot
The seed coat softens and bursts
The radicle emerges and forms the first root
correctOrder: The seed absorbs water through the micropyle
The seed coat softens and bursts
The radicle emerges and forms the first root
The plumule grows to form the shoot

sequencingActivity.explanation: The seed absorbs water through the micropyle, the seed coat softens and bursts, the radicle emerges to form the first root, the plumule grows into the shoot and a seedling develops.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: An orchard owner wants every new tree to bear exactly the same high-quality fruit as the best tree already growing. Which method suits best, and why?

options: Growing from seeds, because seeds always give identical trees
Grafting, because the desired variety is attached to an ordinary plant
Cross-pollination, because it removes all variation
Parthenocarpy, because it makes seeds larger

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Grafting joins a branch of the desired variety to an ordinary plant, so the variety and quality of the fruit are kept; seeds come from sexual reproduction and give variation.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A bread mould survives a long hot, dry spell and then spreads quickly when conditions improve. Which feature of its reproduction best explains this?

options: Thick-walled spores resist adverse environmental conditions
Binary fission halves the size of the cell
Pollen tubes carry sperms to the egg
Cloning uses tissues placed in a medium

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Rhizopus reproduces by spore formation; the thick walls of the spores make them resistant to adverse conditions until favourable conditions return.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A flower has no scent or nectar, small smooth winged pollen, feathery stigmas and large anthers on long stalks. How is it most likely pollinated?

options: By insects, like rose or orchids
By self-pollination only, inside the bud
By wind, like grasses, oak or poplar

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: These are the adaptations of wind-pollinated flowers such as conifers, grasses, cereals, poplar, oak and walnut; insect-pollinated flowers have coloured petals, fragrance and nectar.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: The diploid megaspore mother cell has 2n chromosomes, so the embryo sac that finally forms from one surviving megaspore is _____ (haploid or diploid).
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Meiosis forms four haploid megaspores; the survivor divides by mitosis, so the embryo sac is haploid (n).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Antiretroviral drugs completely cure AIDS by destroying HIV in the body.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: There is no cure for HIV or AIDS; antiretroviral drugs only hinder the growth of HIV.
